title: Russia Welcomes India's Ceasefire Push as Kyiv Weighs Truce Proposal
excerpt: Kyiv called India’s proposal the broadest of four ceasefire offers, covering energy infrastructure and the Black Sea — as Moscow publicly embraced New Delhi’s diplomatic role.
body:
• Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha confirmed Kyiv has received four ceasefire proposals — from India, Turkiye, Egypt and the United States — and called India's "the broadest." Kyiv is ready to consider an energy and Black Sea truce "in this combination."
  • Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the Valdai Discussion Club that Prime Minister Narendra Modi "constantly raises the issue" of ending the conflict at every meeting between the two leaders, and praised his "very good ideas aimed at finding mutually acceptable solutions," according to TASS.
  • Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Moscow welcomes India's willingness to contribute to the peace process, noting New Delhi's position on the conflict corresponds closely with Russia's own.
  • This is a genuine bilateral escalation of India's diplomatic role: it follows India's "beyond advocacy" positioning and adds formal welcomes from both Moscow and Kyiv to the same initiative.

Russia has publicly welcomed India's diplomatic push to end the Ukraine war, as Kyiv confirmed it is weighing New Delhi's proposal for a ceasefire covering energy infrastructure and the Black Sea. The dual endorsement — from Moscow and Kyiv in the same week — marks the most concrete international reception yet for India's mediation efforts.

What India's proposal contains

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Kyiv had received four proposals for a possible ceasefire from India, Turkiye, Egypt and the United States. "We have four proposals. The broadest one is India's proposal. We are ready for an energy and Black Sea ceasefire, but only in this combination," Sybiha said in Kyiv.

The Indian proposal stands out because of its scope. While ceasefire talks have often focused on halting frontline combat, Kyiv wants any agreement to also cover attacks on energy and port infrastructure and the situation in the Black Sea — currently one of the world's most dangerous commercial shipping zones, where both sides have escalated missile and drone strikes against ports, infrastructure and merchant vessels.

Moscow's welcome

Sybiha's statement came a day after Russian President Vladimir Putin praised Prime Minister Narendra Modi's settlement ideas at the annual meeting of the Valdai International Discussion Club, according to state-run TASS.

"He constantly raises the issue of ending the conflict and brings it up at every meeting. He has very good ideas aimed at finding mutually acceptable solutions."

— Vladimir Putin, on Prime Minister Narendra Modi, at the Valdai Discussion Club, per TASS

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, speaking via a virtual briefing from Moscow, underlined that Russia seeks a settlement through peaceful means and is open to such a process. "We know the position of India on the Ukrainian conflict, and to a great extent, it corresponds with our own position," Peskov said. "We welcome the willingness of the Indian side to contribute."

The public warmth follows a round of direct engagement: Putin and Modi held talks ahead of the BRICS summit in New Delhi last month, during which the Russian leader briefed the Prime Minister on the conflict and ongoing peace initiatives. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar separately visited Ukraine recently, discussing peace overtures and Black Sea security directly with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Sybiha.

Impact and analysis

India's appeal as a mediator rests on a rare asset: genuinely open channels to both capitals. New Delhi has bought Russian oil through the war while deepening ties with Kyiv — a position most Western capitals cannot replicate. Having both sides now publicly acknowledge the Indian channel gives the proposal a legitimacy few other initiatives enjoy.

But the gap between a welcome and a settlement remains wide. Sybiha's condition — an energy and Black Sea truce only as a package — and Peskov's careful framing of "openness to the process" both stop well short of commitments on the conflict's hardest questions: occupied territory and sovereign borders. Those will be the ultimate test of Indian diplomacy, and neither Moscow nor Kyiv has moved an inch on them in public.

Diaspora angle

For Indians abroad, the development is watched on two levels: strategic, as a marker of India's rising diplomatic weight; and practical, since progress toward a ceasefire would ease the energy-price and supply-chain shocks that have rippled through diaspora households since 2022.

What's next

Watch whether Moscow moves from welcoming India's "willingness to contribute" to engaging with the proposal's substance — and whether Kyiv's openness to an energy and Black Sea truce survives contact with Russian conditions. The next Modi-Putin bilateral will be the clearest signal of how far this initiative can travel.
